transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, doctor. Well, I'm here because... it's getting really hard to do my work. Every time I have to get near a scaffold, or a roof edge, or some kind of upper platform now, my head just tells me I'm about to go over. 

And the thing is, I can see the rails are in place. I know the setup is supposed to be completely safe, but... I just can't shake that feeling that I'm going to fall.
When you're on that scaffold or platform, do you ever get repeated thoughts or images about yourself falling or jumping, even though you don't actually want to do that?

No, it's not really like that. I don't get... pictures in my head of me jumping or anything. I definitely don't want to jump. It's just this intense, overwhelming feeling that I'm going to slip or the structure is going to give way and I'll fall. It's a physical reaction more than... a specific thought or image playing in my mind.
When you're on these platforms or scaffolds and get that overwhelming feeling, do you also experience physical symptoms like a racing heart, sweating, shortness of breath, or chest tightness?

Yeah, definitely. The second I step onto temporary stairs, or... or even just walk toward an open upper floor, my chest gets really tight. My hands get wet with sweat, and... honestly, I feel like my legs might just lock up completely before I can even make myself take another step. It's an immediate physical reaction.

When you're not on these platforms or scaffolds, do you find yourself avoiding situations where you might encounter heights—like taking different routes to avoid upper floors, or turning down work assignments that involve them?

Yeah, I've started doing that a lot. I've been handing off the height inspections to my foremen whenever I can. And if we need to have a meeting, I make sure we do it down on the ground level. If I absolutely have to go up there... I make sure I have someone right beside me, and I just rush through it as fast as possible. I'm pretty much terrified the entire time I'm up there.

latest_inference.note: Ruled out F40.00 (agoraphobia). Patient's symptoms are specific to heights with clear panic symptoms (chest tightness, sweating, leg weakness) and avoidance behavior. The absence of intrusive thoughts about jumping/falling and emphasis on fear of accidental falling (not self-harm) confirms specific phobia of heights (acrophobia) rather than agoraphobia.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with persistent, intense fear of heights triggered by exposure to elevated platforms and scaffolds in a work setting.
